A petition has been received from\u202FMel Higgins requesting that Council\u202Finclude a fourth option for the Stroud Street Masterplan. The fourth option proposes to retain the existing streetscape of Stroud Street North by maintaining the existing street; continuing routine maintenance of roads, footpaths, verges and street trees; providing project costs and ongoing maintenance costs before proceeding; protecting parking, vehicle access and property functionality; and giving residents the choice to retain what they already have.


Moved: Councillor Senthil Chidambaranathan
Seconded: Councillor Peter Ppiros

Motion

  1. That the petition be received and notes it will be included as part of the consultation feedback report from the Stroud Street Masterplan Community Engagement.

  2. That the requests contained in the petition be considered as part of the development of revised options for next stage of community engagement on the Stroud Street Masterplan.

  3. That a report be tabled at the Strategic Engagement Committee at the conclusion of the next stage of community engagement.

  4. That Council notify the head petitioner of Council’s decision.
 
Carried Unanimously

A Motion on Notice has been received from Councillor Katriona Kinsella seeking the Mayor and Chief Executive Officer to write to the Premier of South Australia regarding the Adelaide Park Lands and John E Brown Park.


Moved: Councillor Katriona Kinsella
Seconded: Councillor Nicholas Le Lacheur

Motion

That the Mayor and the Chief Executive Officer of the City of Charles Sturt jointly write to the Premier of South Australia about the North Adelaide Public Golf Course redevelopment to:

  1. Affirm the importance of protecting the environmental, cultural and heritage values of the Adelaide Park Lands for all South Australians, including for those residing in the City of Charles Sturt;

  2. Affirm that residents of the City of Charles Sturt are frequent users of the Adelaide Park Lands and that it is an important contributor to recreation, tree canopy, habitat and biodiversity within the region, including John E. Brown Park;

  3. Request that the Premier urgently make available information about the redevelopment of John E. Brown Park, with sufficient detail on engagement with Traditional Owners; environmental, heritage and planning assessments; tree canopy protection and biodiversity outcomes including the specific trees to be removed; public access and associated infrastructure; and the retention and protection of the Deceased Workers Memorial Forest (as outlined in the Preamble); and

  4. Further, request that the Premier make available information about successive developments or redevelopments in the Adelaide Park Lands, with sufficient detail about impacts on tree canopy, urban heat and biodiversity; engagement with Traditional Owners; consistency with the National Heritage listing and the progress of the UNESCO World Heritage Bid; and measures in place to mitigate any impacts (as outlined in the Preamble).
Carried Unanimously

In accordance with the Local Government Act 1999 the CEO is recommending that this report be heard in confidence under Section 90(3)(b)(i) and (ii) and 90(3)(d)(i) and (ii) as information the disclosure of which could reasonably be expected to confer a commercial advantage on a person with whom the council is conducting, or proposing to conduct, business, or to prejudice the commercial position of the council; and would, on balance, be contrary to the public interest. b.

The City of Charles Sturt acknowledges and pays respect to the traditional custodians of the land, the Kaurna people of the Adelaide plains. We pay our respect to Elders past, present and emerging. We respect their spiritual beliefs and connections to land which are of continuing importance to the Kaurna people of today. We acknowledge the contributions and important role that Aboriginal people continue to play within our local community in Charles Sturt. We also respect the culture of Aboriginal people visiting from other areas of South Australia and Australia.

Almighty Father from Whom all goodness flows, grant unto us qualities of wisdom justice and tolerance, that we the civic leaders of this community may govern in harmony and concord.

This we ask in Thy name. 

We also remember and give thanks for those, our sons and daughters, who gave their lives for Australia. 

Lest we forget. 

Councillor - Nicholas Le Lacheur entered the meeting at 7:01 PM.

Motion

  1. That the report be received and noted.

  2. That Dr Matthew Ward and Ms Nicole Pelton be thanked for their presentation and the presentation be included in the minutes.

  3. That the Mayor write to the Minister for Climate, Environment and Water expressing Council's concern regarding the proposed sediment rehandling methodology for the Adelaide Beach Management Review Phase II dredging program. The letter should state that:

    1. Council does not support the use of West Beach or Henley Beach South as sediment rehandling sites, either for the proposed trial or as a long-term proposal, due to the potential environmental impacts on Posidonia seagrass meadows, water quality, and the marine environment.

    2. Alternative sand placement methods that minimise or avoid impacts on Posidonia seagrass meadows should be fully considered before any future dredging-based replenishment program is adopted.

    3. Future sand replenishment programs should prioritise recycling sand from the Northern Beaches into the Central Beaches coastal system, rather than relocating sand from within the Central Beaches system.

Leave of the meeting was sought for Dr Matthew Ward and Ms Nicole Pelton to provide further clarification on any queries. Leave was granted.

This report presents the outcomes of Stage Two Community Engagement undertaken to validate and refine the preferred Master Plan Concept (Scenario 3 - Revised) for the Jubilee Reserve Redevelopment.

Feedback from stakeholders and the broader community has informed further development of the Final Master Plan, including consideration of key matters such as sports field configuration, fencing, accessibility and shared use of the reserve. These outcomes, together with the Federal Government’s $5 million funding commitment, provide the basis for Council’s consideration of the final concept design and authorisation to accept the funding offer and enter into a funding agreement for delivery of the project.


Material Declaration of Interest

Councillor - Stuart Ghent declared a material conflict of interest pursuant to Section 75C of the Local Government Act for Item 6.2. The nature of Councillor - Stuart Ghent's material conflict is that a family member owns home on the north westerly end of Hawkesbury Way, West Lakes Shore. He regularly walks a family member's dog on Jubilee Reserve, but not when organised sport is played on this Reserve. Councillor - Stuart Ghent dealt with this conflict by leaving the meeting.

Councillor - Stuart Ghent left the meeting at 9:56 PM.

General Declaration of Interest

Councillor - Nicholas Le Lacheur declared a general conflict of interest pursuant to Section 75B of the Local Government Act for Item 6.2. The nature of Councillor - Nicholas Le Lacheur's general conflict is that his house is nearby Jubilee Reserve and within the consultation zone, which could be interpreted as a benefit if the upgrade project goes ahead. This is not a material conflict because it comes under Section 75A(1)(a) of the Act as the same interest is shared with a large proportion of his constituents within the Semaphore Park area. Councillor - Nicholas Le Lacheur dealt with the conflict of interest in the following transparent and accountable way and remained in the meeting, participating in the debate and voting.


Moved: Councillor Nicholas Le LacheurSeconded: Councillor Peter Ppiros

Motion

To complete the master planning phase of the Jubilee Reserve Redevelopment and enable progression to detailed design and construction, that Council:

  1. Receives and notes the Stage Two Community Engagement Summary Report, as detailed in Appendix 1.

  2. Endorses the Final Master Plan for the Jubilee Reserve Redevelopment, as detailed in Appendix 2 (page 4), as the basis for project delivery, noting that it has been developed having regard to:

    1. the feedback from site users and the community received through Stages One and Two of Council's Community Engagement Approach;
    2. the previously endorsed Scenario 3 (revised) Master Plan Concept; and
    3. the requirements associated with the Federal Government funding offer through the Major and Local Community Infrastructure Program.

  3. Notes that, concurrent with the Jubilee Reserve Redevelopment, the school oval partnership with West Lakes Primary School, has now been endorsed by the school governing council and contributes significantly to providing increased opportunity to participate in turf sport and recreation within the precinct.

  4. Authorises the Chief Executive Officer and as necessary the Mayor to enter into and execute a $5,000,000 funding agreement with the Federal Government, including attaching the Council seal if required.

  5. That throughout the detailed design process we communicate in good faith with the community and key stakeholders. 
Carried

Division called by Councillor Nicole Mazeika

Voters
For:Councillor - Alice Campbell, Councillor -Senthil Chidambaranathan, Councillor -Nicholas Le Lacheur, Councillor -Nicole Mazeika, Councillor - Peter Ppiros, Councillor - Tom Scheffler, Councillor - Quin Tran, Councillor - Rachele Tullio (8)
Against:Councillor - Merlindie Fardone, Councillor - Kelly Thomas, George Turelli, Councillor - Kenzie van den Nieuwelaar (4)
Not Vote:Mayor Angela Evans (1)
The Motion to Item 6.2. was Carried

Councillor - Stuart Ghent entered the meeting at 10:47 PM.

  2. That Council endorse the transitionally updated Discretionary Ward Allowance Guidelines as detailed in Appendix 2, and that following the Local Government Elections in April 2027, that the transitional text be removed by administration.
 

Carried Unanimously

The Strategic and Engagement Committee was held on Monday, 20 July 2026.


Moved: Councillor Nicole MazeikaSeconded: Councillor Nicholas Le Lacheur

That having considered the recommendations of the Committee which has read and considered the reports in the agenda related to items:

 

4.1 GRANT OF EASEMENT - SA POWER NETWORKS - GRANGE RECREATION RESERVE
 
Motion
  
  1. That Council consent to the granting of an easement over Lot 34 in Filed Plan 118716 (Certificate of Title Vol 4101 Fol 209) as shown in Appendix 2.
 
  1. That Council delegates authority to the Chief Executive Officer to deal with all conveyancing transactions and to sign all documents and provide such information as required to deliver Recommendation 1.
 
 4.2 COMMUNTY CONSULTATION FOR EASEMENT REQUEST - HERO WAY, WEST LAKES
 
Motion
  
  1. That Council acknowledge receipt of the formal request by Mr Dennis Chung of IBS Planning and Projects (Appendix 1).
 
  1. That Council endorse a Community Engagement Approach (Appendix 4) and undertake consultation on the proposal to grant a right of way access across the Council reserve Allotment 87 in Deposited Plan 18539 (CT Vol 5546 Fol 412).
 
  1. That the consultation outcomes be presented to Council in a future report for further decision making.
 
 4.3 STUDENT ACCOMMODATION DEVELOPMENT - POLICY FRAMEWORK AND DEVELOPMENT ACTIVITY REVIEW
 
Motion
  
  1. That the report be received and noted.
 
 4.4 CONSULTATION OUTCOMES - REQUEST TO AMEND COMMUNITY LAND MANAGEMENT PLAN - MIRANI COURT RESERVE, WEST LAKES SHORE 
 
Motion
  
  1. That the Community Engagement Summary Report (Appendix 1) relating to the proposed amendment to the Mirani Court Reserve Community Land Management Plan be received and noted.
 
  1. That Council notes the outcomes of the community engagement process and the feedback received from stakeholders and the community, specifically that 170 submissions were received during the community consultation process, including 164 submissions (96%) supporting the proposed amendment, 5 submissions (3%) opposing the proposed amendment and 1 submission (1%) indicating uncertainty.
 
  1. That pursuant to section 198 of the Local Government Act 1999, Council adopts the amended Mirani Court Reserve Community Land Management Plan as contained in Appendix 2.
 
  1. That public notice, pursuant to section 198(4) of the Local Government Act 1999, be made confirming the adoption of the amended Mirani Court Reserve Community Land Management Plan.

 

Council adopts the recommendations of the Committee as printed in the Minutes of this Committee.

Carried Unanimously

The Operations Committee was held on Monday, 20 July 2026.


Moved: Councillor Senthil ChidambaranathanSeconded: Councillor Tom Scheffler

That having considered the recommendations of the Committee which has read and considered the reports in the agenda related to items:

 

4.1 PRESENTATION - ALTERNATIVE WATER SUPPLY EFFICIENCY MEASURES UPDATE
 
Motion
  
 That the Committee recommends to the Council:
 
  1. That the report be received and noted.
 
  1. That staff be thanked for their presentation and that a copy of the presentation be included in the minutes.
 
 4.2 CITY OPERATIONS CAPITAL WORKS & OPERATING PROGRAM VARIATIONS
 
Motion
  
 That the Committee recommends to the Council: 
 
  1. That the following variations to the Capital Works and Annual Operating Program be approved and budgets or scope adjusted accordingly:
 
  1. Budgeted expenditure for Solar Panels, Batteries and Energy Management Equipment (Project 3599 - New) be increased by $375,375 from savings in the New Viewing Platform in Mirani Court (Project 3664 - New).

  2. Budgeted expenditure for SGF - West Lakes Smosh Clubroom Upgrade (Project 3343 - New) be increased by $20,000 from savings in the New Viewing Platform in Mirani Court (Project 3664 - New).
     
  3. Budgeted expenditure for Road Rehabilitation Program 2025/26-Robert ST-with Elizabeth (Project 3721 - Renewal) be increased by $250,000 from savings in the Living Streets Road Reconstruction and Streetscape Program (Project 3542 - Renewal).
     
  4. Budgeted expenditure for Major Streetscape Projects - Masterplan Package (Project 3955 - Upgrade) remain unchanged, with the project scope change to include the Morley Road, Seaton Corridor works.
 
4.3 PROPOSED ROAD NAME CHANGE - SECTION OF BIRDSONG AVENUE, KIDMAN PARK TO ST JAMES PARKWAY, KIDMAN PARK 
 
Motion
  
 That the Committee recommends to the Council:
 
  1. That the report be received and noted.
 
  1. That the consultation approach of ‘inform’, as outlined in the Community Engagement Approach (Appendix 1), be noted.
 
  1. That the section of Birdsong Avenue, Kidman Park be renamed to St James Parkway, Kidman Park.
 
  1. That in line with the Road Naming and Premises Numbering Policy, notice of this Council resolution be given to appropriate authorities in writing, and to the public in the form of a public notice in the Government Gazette and the Advertiser.

 

Council adopts the recommendations of the Committee as printed in the Minutes of this Committee.


                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 Carried Unanimously


Councillor - Quin Tran entered the meeting at 7:06 PM.

Councillor Alice Campbell has given notice in accordance with the Local Government (Procedures at Meetings) Regulations 2013 that she will ask a number of Questions on Notice relation to the use of glyphosate on verges, parks, and other green spaces at this meeting. 


Questions
  1. Can Council be advised on our approach in the use of glyphosate for managing weeds on our verges, parks and other green spaces? This includes schedules for weed spraying and if contractors are used. If contractors are used, do they have to comply with rules set out by Council, such as to how to use the equipment most effectively and avoid spraying unnecessary amounts.

  2. Can Council further advise if alternatives to glyphosate have been considered and the reasons for its continued use?


Questions and Answers
  1. Can Council be advised on our approach in the use of glyphosate for managing weeds on our verges, parks and other green spaces? This includes schedules for weed spraying and if contractors are used. If contractors are used, do they have to comply with rules set out by Council, such as to how to use the equipment most effectively and avoid spraying unnecessary amounts.

 

The City of Charles Sturt uses glyphosate as one of a range of tools to manage weeds across road verges, reserves, parks, streetscapes and other Council-managed open spaces. Its use forms part of an integrated weed management approach aimed at maintaining safe, accessible and well-presented public spaces while protecting community assets and minimising environmental impacts. Council is currently transitioning from a largely reactive weed management model to a planned, intelligence-based maintenance program. Rather than responding only to visible weed outbreaks or customer requests, weed control activities are now programmed, monitored and reviewed through scheduled inspections and recorded treatment data.

This approach is supported by Council's new broadleaf spray unit fitted with an integrated GPS mapping system. Every spray application is digitally recorded, including the treatment location, application rate and area covered. This technology enables Council to:

  • Monitor treatment locations and coverage.
  • Prevent unnecessary overlap and duplicate applications.
  • Assess treatment effectiveness over time.
  • Improve planning and programming of future weed management.
  • Reduce unnecessary herbicide use through targeted application.



Within turf areas, selective broadleaf herbicides are used where appropriate to control invasive weeds while retaining desirable turf species. Following treatment, temporary patchiness may occur as weeds die before the surrounding turf naturally recovers. Council also continues to invest in preventative turf management practices that reduce long-term weed establishment. This includes the introduction of specialised turf aeration equipment to relieve soil compaction, improve root health and increase turf density. Healthier turf provides greater natural competition against weeds, reducing the need for future chemical intervention. Chemical edge treatments may also be used in specific circumstances where turf encroachment occurs onto footpaths, kerbs and other infrastructure, particularly during periods of increased irrigation or seasonal growth. These treatments are applied only where required to protect infrastructure and maintain accessibility.

Council undertakes programmed weed control throughout the year, with treatment timing determined by:

  • Seasonal weed growth.
  • Weather conditions.
  • Asset type.
  • Irrigation requirements.
  • Site inspections.
  • Recorded treatment history.
  • Service level priorities.

Broadleaf weed control programs are generally undertaken during periods when weeds are actively growing to maximise effectiveness and reduce the need for repeat applications.

Council conducts weed control activities using both Council staff and contractors. Council staff conducting weed control activities are suitably qualified and licensed, and when Council engages contractors for weed control, they are also suitably qualified and licensed to undertake weed control activities across the City. All contractors are required to comply with the same legislative requirements, Council specifications and operational standards as Council staff. This includes compliance with Council's Standard Work Procedures and Safe Operating Procedures for herbicide application. These requirements include:

  • Applying herbicides only to target weeds rather than blanket spraying.
  • Using the correct herbicide and application rate in accordance with manufacturer instructions.
  • Maintaining spray equipment to ensure accurate application.
  • Minimising spray drift by using appropriate nozzles and keeping spray close to the target.
  • Ceasing spraying when weather conditions exceed operational limits, including temperatures above 30°C, wind speeds greater than 15 km/h or unsuitable Delta T conditions.
  • Immediately stopping spraying whenever members of the public enter the work area and maintaining a minimum separation distance before recommencing work.
  • Installing appropriate warning signage advising that herbicide spraying is in progress.
  • Wearing appropriate personal protective equipment and following all Safety Data Sheet (SDS) requirements.

    Council also maintains a "No Herbicide Use" register for residents with specific health concerns or sensitivities. Where appropriate, operational staff review this register before commencing programmed spraying activities. Overall, Council's objective is to use the minimum amount of herbicide necessary to achieve effective weed control while protecting public safety, the environment and surrounding vegetation.

 

  1. Can Council further advise if alternatives to glyphosate have been considered and the reasons for its continued use?

 

Council continually monitors developments in weed management and remains open to practical, safe and environmentally responsible alternatives to glyphosate. Alternative weed control methods currently used include:

  • Manual hand weeding.
  • Mechanical weed removal.
  • Turf renovation and aeration.
  • Improved irrigation management.
  • Increasing turf density to naturally suppress weed establishment.
  • Mulching in garden beds to reduce weed germination.

    While these methods are appropriate in many locations, they are not suitable or effective for all weed control situations across more than 1,300 hectares of Council-managed parks, reserves and road verges. Council's continued use of glyphosate is based on several considerations:

  • It remains registered for use by the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority (APVMA).
  • It has been assessed by the Australian Government as safe when used in accordance with approved label directions and regulatory requirements.
  • It provides effective control of invasive weeds with relatively low application rates.
  • Targeted application reduces disturbance to soils and surrounding vegetation compared with some mechanical methods.
  • It remains one of the most practical and cost-effective tools available for managing weeds across large public open spaces.

 

Council will continue to review emerging research, regulatory advice and new technologies as they become available. Where practical, safe and economically sustainable alternatives demonstrate equal or improved effectiveness, Council will consider incorporating them into its integrated weed management program. Council remains committed to continually improving its weed management practices by balancing environmental responsibility, worker safety, public safety, operational effectiveness and responsible use of public resources.

The City of Charles Sturt acknowledges and pays respect to the traditional custodians of the land, the Kaurna people of the Adelaide plains. We pay our respect to Elders past, present and emerging. We respect their spiritual beliefs and connections to land which are of continuing importance to the Kaurna people of today. We acknowledge the contributions and important role that Aboriginal people continue to play within our local community in Charles Sturt. We also respect the culture of Aboriginal people visiting from other areas of South Australia and Australia.

Almighty Father from Whom all goodness flows, grant unto us qualities of wisdom justice and tolerance, that we the civic leaders of this community may govern in harmony and concord.

This we ask in Thy name. 

We also remember and give thanks for those, our sons and daughters, who gave their lives for Australia. 

Lest we forget.

  1. That Council endorse the key principles in Appendix 1 to inform the City of Charles Sturt's response to the State Government consultation on personal mobility devices and e-bike laws.

  3. That a copy of the correspondence be provided to the Local Government Association to inform its sector wide response to the State Government consultation.

Carried Unanimously

The Corporate Services Committee was held on Monday, 3 August 2026.


Moved: Councillor Michael McEwenSeconded: Councillor Nicholas Le Lacheur

That having considered the recommendations of the Committee which has read and considered the reports in the agenda related to all items, with the exception of Item 4.1:

 

4.2. - POLICY REVIEW - FINANCIAL POLICIES
  
 Motion
  
 That the Committee recommends to the Council:
  
  1. That the annual review of Council financial policies, such review not precluding any subsequent review, alteration or additional policy which Council may wish to make from time to time, be adopted.  
 
  1. That the specific policies as amended through track changes and detailed in Appendices 1 through 15 to the report be endorsed and adopted and incorporated into Council's Policy Register.
 
  1. That the Restricted Assets Policy (Appendix 16) be revoked, as it has been combined with the Statutory Financial Reporting Policy (Appendix 15).
 
  1. That the review schedules of financial policies be updated from annually to every two years, to align with the review frequency of other Council policies and procedures, with the next review date updated to August 2028 if adopted for Appendices 1-15.
 
  1. The Corporate Services Committee notes that the Financial Policies were circulated to the Audit and Risk Committee for review, with no further feedback received.
 
 4.3. - POLICY REVIEW - COUNCIL MEMBER LEGAL ADVICE POLICY
  
 Motion
  
 That the Committee recommends to the Council:
  
  1. That the Committee recommends to the Council that the updated Council Member Legal Advice Policy (Appendix 1) be adopted.
  
 4.4. - POLICY REVIEW - SPORTING AND COMMUNITY CLUBS FEES POLICY
  
 Motion
  
That Council endorse for community consultation the proposed Sporting and Community Clubs Fees Policy, which responds to the impacts of the statutory building revaluation by increasing the maximum Social Benefit Discount and introducing a contemporary, outcomes-based framework that better aligns Council's financial support with the community outcomes delivered by sporting and community clubs, by:
  
  1. Endorsing the draft Sporting and Community Clubs Fees Policy (Appendix 1) for community consultation in accordance with the Community Engagement Approach (Appendix 2).
 
  1. Receiving a further report following completion of community consultation for consideration of stakeholder feedback and final policy adoption.
 
 4.5. - POLICY REVIEW - AGEING IN CHARLES STURT POLICY
  
 Motion
  
 That the Committee recommends to the Council:
  
  1. That the amendments to the Ageing in Charles Sturt Policy align with Council's transition away from Commonwealth Home Support Program delivery.
 
  1. That the amendments to the Ageing in Charles Sturt Policy align with the City of Charles Sturt's Ageing Well model.
 
 4.6. - POLICY REVIEW - DISPOSAL OF ASSET POLICY
  
 Motion
 
 That the Committee recommends to the Council:
  
  1. That the Committee recommends to Council that the updated Disposal of Asset Policy (Appendix 1) be adopted.
 
 4.7. – POLICIES FOR REVIEW – MINOR CHANGES ONLY
  
 Motion
  
 That the Committee recommends to the Council that: 
  
  1. The Commonwealth Home Support Programme Fees Policy (Appendix 1) be revoked. 
 
  1. The revised policies below be adopted:
 
  • Council Member Access to Information Policy (Appendix 2)
  • Council Policy Framework (Appendix 3) 
  • Healthy Food and Drink Choices Policy (Appendix 4)
  • Privacy Policy (Appendix 5)
  • Prudential Review Policy (Appendix 6)
  • Sports Awards Event Sponsorship Policy (Appendix 7)
  

Council adopts the recommendations of the Committee as printed in the Minutes of this Committee.

Carried Unanimously


Moved: Councillor Michael McEwenSeconded: Councillor Nicholas Le Lacheur

4.1. - UPDATE TO FEES AND CHARGES REGISTER 2026/27
 
Motion

  1. That the amendments to the Fees and Charges Register 2026/27 be endorsed as identified in Appendix 1 and 2, with the following amendment:
    1. That the Dog Registration fees table be updated with the highlighted rows below:


Carried Unanimously

To advise Council Members of the 2026 Local Government Finance Authority of South Australia (LGFA) Annual General Meeting to be held on Friday 4 December 2026, to appoint a Council representative, and a call for motions and nominations for the Board of Trustees.



Moved: Councillor Senthil Chidambaranathan
Seconded: Councillor Edgar Agius

Motion

  1. That Council notes the arrangements for the Annual General Meeting of the Local Government Finance Authority of South Australia (LGFA) to be held on Friday 4 December 2026.

  2. That Council appoints Mayor Evans as its representative for the 2026 LGFA Annual General Meeting.

  3. That if any member of Council wishes to place a Notice of Motion on the agenda for the 2026 LGFA Annual General Meeting, a draft Notice of Motion must be submitted to the Chief Executive by Monday 17 August 2026.

  4. That Council does not make a nomination for the Local Government Finance Authority Board of Trustees.

[OUTLINE_NUMBER_FULL_NO_PERIOD][AGENDA_ITEM_NAME][IGNORE_INDENT][NOTE]
Brief
[ITEM_DESCRIPTION]
","reportContent":null,"minutesDiscussion":"Brief
Questions on Notices have been received from Councillor Kelly Thomas in relation to illegal dumping incidents, enforcement, and operational impacts, in light of community concerns regarding increased levels of illegal dumping across the City of Charles Sturt.


Questions
  1. Enforcement & Returning Waste to Offenders

  1. In cases where illegal dumpers are successfully identified, does Council exercise powers to order or require the returning of illegally dumped waste back to the offender’s property, or seek full cost recovery for clearance and disposal?

  2. Over the past 12 months (or most recent financial year), how many instances of illegal dumping resulted in direct cost recovery or forced removal orders issued to the perpetrator?

  1. Fines and Expiation Notices

  1. How many Expiation Notices (fines) or compliance orders were issued by Council officers for illegal dumping and littering under the Local Nuisance and Litter Control Act 2016 over the last 12 to 24 months?

  2. What is the total monetary value of fines issued for illegal dumping during this period, and what proportion of these fines has been successfully collected?

  1. Volume and Direct Cost to Council

  1. What total tonnage/volume of illegally dumped waste was collected and disposed of by Council staff or contractors over the last financial year?

  2. What was the total financial cost incurred by Council (including staff labor, tipping/waste transfer fees, equipment, and contractor costs) to collect and process this dumped waste?

  1. Investigation Timelines & Enforcement Efficiency

  1. What is the average timeframe from when an illegal dumping report is logged (e.g., via the Customer Portal, My Local Services app, or Snap Send Solve) to the completion of the investigation?

  2. What is the average turnaround time between a report being lodged and the physical clearance of the dumped waste from public land?

  1. Year-on-Year Trend Analysis & Comparative Impact

  1. How do the total recorded illegal dumping incidents across the City of Charles Sturt over the past 12 months compare to the previous 12-month period (e.g., breakdown of Non-Safety Risk vs. Public Safety Risk incidents)?

  2. What was the total financial expenditure (processing, cleanup, and enforcement) incurred by Council for illegal dumping in the past 12 months, and how does this figure compare to the previous 12-month financial year?

  3. Has Administration identified any specific hotspots, recurring illegal dumping categories (e.g., hard waste, construction material, commercial dumping), or emerging trends over the last year driving this increase?

  4. What specific proactive steps, CCTV surveillance measures, or targeted enforcement campaigns are currently planned or being implemented to reverse this trajectory?


Questions and Answers
  1. Enforcement & Returning Waste to Offenders

 

  1. In cases where illegal dumpers are successfully identified, does Council exercise powers to order or require the returning of illegally dumped waste back to the offender’s property, or seek full cost recovery for clearance and disposal?

    Where sufficient evidence exists to identify a responsible person, Council may utilise enforcement options available under the\u202FLocal Nuisance and Litter Control Act 2016, including the issuing of Expiation Notices and Abatement Notices requiring the removal of unlawfully deposited material. Enforcement action is determined on a case-by-case basis having regard to the available evidence and circumstances of each matter. Council's focus is on securing compliance and preventing further offending in line with Council's Enforcement Policy. 

    While cost recovery may be available in some circumstances, opportunities are generally limited and Council's response is often focused on timely removal of waste to maintain public amenity and safety. 

 

  1. Over the past 12 months (or most recent financial year), how many instances of illegal dumping resulted in direct cost recovery or forced removal orders issued to the perpetrator?

 

A previous review of illegal dumping activities over a two-year period identified 254 instances where rubbish was reclaimed or "taken back" rather than being removed by Council. This represented approximately 3% of the 8,179 illegal dumping related cases received during the same two year period. 

 

More recent analysis of 4,719 illegal dumping related cases between 1 March 2025 and 2 March 2026 identified 147 "take-back" outcomes, representing 3.1% of all cases. These figures demonstrate that while compliance and enforcement remain important tools, opportunities to identify a responsible person and secure a take-back outcome remain relatively limited when compared with the overall volume of illegal dumping incidents.

 

 

  1. Fines and Expiation Notices

 

  1. How many Expiation Notices (fines) or compliance orders were issued by Council officers for illegal dumping and littering under the Local Nuisance and Litter Control Act 2016 over the last 12 to 24 months?

 

A previous review undertaken by Administration identified that 36 infringement notices were issued for littering offences under the\u202FLocal Nuisance and Litter Control Act 2016\u202Fover a two-year period. Council's Annual Report data also records the following expiated offences relating to disposal of Class B hazardous or general litter exceeding 50 litres and this shows in the 2024-2025 financial year, six expiations were issued compared to eight in the 2025-2026 financial year for these offences. The Class B hazardous or general litter exceeding 50 litres expiation numbers are included in the 36 infringements for that period. 

 

Council also utilises a range of compliance tools including education, warnings, investigations, abatement notices, take-back actions and expiations where appropriate. 

 

  1. What is the total monetary value of fines issued for illegal dumping during this period, and what proportion of these fines has been successfully collected?

 

A review of infringement activity identified that over a recent two year period: 

 

  • 36 infringement notices were issued;
  • 16 were paid;
  • 10 were referred to the Fines Enforcement and Recovery Unit (FERU);
  • 2 remained in progress; and
  • 8 were waived.


Infringement amounts vary depending on the nature and severity of the offence and may be either $210 or $1,000. 


The total value paid or payable from these infringement notices was reported as $20,890. 


While infringement notices form an important component of Council's compliance response, enforcement outcomes remain dependent on the availability of evidence sufficient to identify a responsible person and support formal action.

 

  1. Volume and Direct Cost to Council

 

  1. What total tonnage/volume of illegally dumped waste was collected and disposed of by Council staff or contractors over the last financial year?

 

Council records illegal dumping incidents and associated clean-up activities; however, tonnage and volume data is not consistently captured across all collection activities. This is because there is no efficient or reliable way to measure the weight or volume of waste from each individual collection. Illegal dumping collections vary significantly, from small items through to larger loads, so measuring each collection would not be practical within current operational arrangements.  

 

For the purpose of providing an indicative volume estimate, if the 4,719 illegal dumping related collections previously reviewed were assumed to average approximately 20 kilograms per collection, this would equate to approximately 95 tonnes of illegally dumped waste. This figure is an estimate only and should not be read as a measured tonnage.

 

  1. What was the total financial cost incurred by Council (including staff labor, tipping/waste transfer fees, equipment, and contractor costs) to collect and process this dumped waste?

 

Illegal dumping imposes a direct financial burden on Council through investigation, collection, disposal and operational response activities. A precise annual cost is not currently available, as costs are not separately captured for every incident and can vary depending on the size, location and type of material collected.

 

Based on the indicative tonnage estimate outlined in 3a, and applying an estimated disposal and transport cost of approximately $300 per tonne, the direct disposal-related cost would be in the order of $28,500. When this is considered together with labour associated with approximately one full-time equivalent resource, equipment, collection activity and related operational costs, the total annual cost to Council is broadly estimated to be in the order of $125,000 to $150,000. 

 

This estimate should be treated as a broad indication only rather than a fully verified annual expenditure figure. Actual costs will vary depending on the nature, size and location of each incident, the volume and type of material collected, disposal pathway, labour and equipment requirements, and whether investigation or enforcement activity is required. 

 

It is also important to note that these figures are indicative and should not be taken to mean that all illegally dumped material is sent to landfill. The majority of this material is directed through Council’s Recycling and Waste Centre, where recyclable items are separated and recycled where possible. Items that are suitable for reuse may also be rehomed through charity or other reuse pathways. Council makes every reasonable effort to recover, recycle or reuse material before disposal, which helps reduce the amount ultimately sent to landfill.

 

  1. Investigation Timelines & Enforcement Efficiency

 

  1. What is the average timeframe from when an illegal dumping report is logged (e.g., via the Customer Portal, My Local Services app, or Snap Send Solve) to the completion of the investigation?

 

Illegal dumping investigations vary significantly depending on the nature of the incident and the availability of evidence. Investigations may include site inspections, collection of evidence, witness statements, examination of dumped materials and engagement with alleged offenders. If an initial assessment determines that an investigation is not warranted and/or the likelihood of determining a responsible person is low, the investigation will be closed in a short time frame and dumped items disposed of. Community Safety Officers are committed to undertaking investigations in a timely manner and aim to have most substantive investigations without significant complexities are completed within 14 days.

 

  1. What is the average turnaround time between a report being lodged and the physical clearance of the dumped waste from public land?

 

Reported dumped waste is prioritised according to risk. Public safety hazards are generally responded to as a priority, while other incidents are assessed based on risk, location, operational considerations and the potential for investigation. For example, if a responsible person has been identified and the rubbish does not pose a public safety risk, the responsible person will be provided the opportunity to reclaim the rubbish which means it will remain on public land while that pursued. 

 

  1. Year-on-Year Trend Analysis & Comparative Impact

 

  1. How do the total recorded illegal dumping incidents across the City of Charles Sturt over the past 12 months compare to the previous 12-month period (e.g., breakdown of Non-Safety Risk vs. Public Safety Risk incidents)?

 

Administration has observed a significant increase in illegal dumping reports across the City and is currently reviewing how this issue is managed. 

 

During the first four months of 2026, Council received 1,209 reports of non-hazardous illegal dumping. By comparison, Council received 2,814 non-hazardous illegal dumping reports across the whole of 2025. 

 

While these figures represent different reporting periods and are not directly comparable, they indicate a substantial increase in demand and reinforce the need to better understand the factors contributing to illegal dumping before determining long-term responses. 

 

Illegal dumping is not unique to the City of Charles Sturt and continues to be a challenge experienced by many metropolitan councils.

 

  1. What was the total financial expenditure (processing, cleanup, and enforcement) incurred by Council for illegal dumping in the past 12 months, and how does this figure compare to the previous 12-month financial year?

 

Administration is currently assessing the operational and financial impacts associated with illegal dumping, including collection, disposal, contractor and enforcement costs. Current general expenditure includes approximately one full-time equivalent resource, together with associated collection activity and waste disposal costs. 
 
Based on the broad waste disposal estimate outlined above, and allowing for the labour associated with a full-time equivalent resource, the indicative annual cost of responding to illegal dumping is likely to be in the order of $125,000 to $150,000 per year. This should be treated as a broad estimate only, rather than a fully verified annual expenditure figure.

 

The operational effort can also shift depending on current dumping rates. When dumping volumes are high, the immediate priority is generally to remove waste from streets and public spaces as quickly as possible to maintain amenity, reduce safety risks and prevent dumped material becoming an eyesore or attracting further dumping. When dumping rates are lower, the team has greater capacity to pivot toward prevention activities, including education, community messaging, hotspot monitoring and targeted engagement to reduce repeat behaviour. This means the overall resource commitment may remain relatively consistent, but the focus of that effort can change depending on demand. Expenditure is generally expected to be reasonably consistent year to year, although some operational costs may fluctuate depending on the number, size and type of dumping incidents, disposal requirements and the extent of investigation or clean-up activity required.  

 

 

  1. Has Administration identified any specific hotspots, recurring illegal dumping categories (e.g., hard waste, construction material, commercial dumping), or emerging trends over the last year driving this increase?

 

Administration has observed a significant increase in illegal dumping reports across the City and is currently reviewing how this issue is managed.

 

While hotspot locations continue to be monitored, the increase appears to be occurring across a broader range of locations rather than being confined to a small number of sites.

 

Because of the observed increase, Council is strengthening its data collection and analysis to better understand:

 

    • the types of materials being dumped;
    • locations and frequency of incidents;
    • emerging behavioural patterns; and
    • factors contributing to the increase.


This information will help inform future prevention, education and compliance initiatives and ensure any proposed response is evidence-based and financially sustainable.

 

  1. What specific proactive steps, CCTV surveillance measures, or targeted enforcement campaigns are currently planned or being implemented to reverse this trajectory?

 

Council is actively adapting its response to the increase in illegal dumping by: 

 

  • increasing collection efforts to maintain community amenity and public safety;
  • collecting more detailed data on dumped material types, locations and frequency;
  • identifying emerging hotspots and changing patterns of behaviour;
  • reviewing education, compliance and enforcement approaches to support behaviour change; and
  • engaging with the local government sector to better understand trends and successful intervention strategies.

 

Council also continues to promote existing disposal options available to residents, including: 

 

  • two free at-call hard waste collections per financial year;
  • free or low-cost disposal options through the Beverley Recycling and Waste Centre for a range of household materials including e-waste, paint, batteries, oils, scrap metal and other recyclable materials; and
  • opportunities to reuse suitable items through local charities and community organisations.

 

Administration's current focus is to better understand the drivers of illegal dumping and develop a coordinated response that balances prevention, education, enforcement and service delivery while remaining financially sustainable.

Questions and Answers
  1. Enforcement & Returning Waste to Offenders

 

  1. In cases where illegal dumpers are successfully identified, does Council exercise powers to order or require the returning of illegally dumped waste back to the offender’s property, or seek full cost recovery for clearance and disposal?

    Where sufficient evidence exists to identify a responsible person, Council may utilise enforcement options available under the\u202FLocal Nuisance and Litter Control Act 2016, including the issuing of Expiation Notices and Abatement Notices requiring the removal of unlawfully deposited material. Enforcement action is determined on a case-by-case basis having regard to the available evidence and circumstances of each matter. Council's focus is on securing compliance and preventing further offending in line with Council's Enforcement Policy. 

    While cost recovery may be available in some circumstances, opportunities are generally limited and Council's response is often focused on timely removal of waste to maintain public amenity and safety. 

 

  1. Over the past 12 months (or most recent financial year), how many instances of illegal dumping resulted in direct cost recovery or forced removal orders issued to the perpetrator?

 

A previous review of illegal dumping activities over a two-year period identified 254 instances where rubbish was reclaimed or \"taken back\" rather than being removed by Council. This represented approximately 3% of the 8,179 illegal dumping related cases received during the same two year period. 

 

More recent analysis of 4,719 illegal dumping related cases between 1 March 2025 and 2 March 2026 identified 147 \"take-back\" outcomes, representing 3.1% of all cases. These figures demonstrate that while compliance and enforcement remain important tools, opportunities to identify a responsible person and secure a take-back outcome remain relatively limited when compared with the overall volume of illegal dumping incidents.

 

 

  1. Fines and Expiation Notices

 

  1. How many Expiation Notices (fines) or compliance orders were issued by Council officers for illegal dumping and littering under the Local Nuisance and Litter Control Act 2016 over the last 12 to 24 months?

 

A previous review undertaken by Administration identified that 36 infringement notices were issued for littering offences under the\u202FLocal Nuisance and Litter Control Act 2016\u202Fover a two-year period. Council's Annual Report data also records the following expiated offences relating to disposal of Class B hazardous or general litter exceeding 50 litres and this shows in the 2024-2025 financial year, six expiations were issued compared to eight in the 2025-2026 financial year for these offences. The Class B hazardous or general litter exceeding 50 litres expiation numbers are included in the 36 infringements for that period. 

 

Council also utilises a range of compliance tools including education, warnings, investigations, abatement notices, take-back actions and expiations where appropriate. 

 

  1. What is the total monetary value of fines issued for illegal dumping during this period, and what proportion of these fines has been successfully collected?

 

A review of infringement activity identified that over a recent two year period: 

 

  • 36 infringement notices were issued;
  • 16 were paid;
  • 10 were referred to the Fines Enforcement and Recovery Unit (FERU);
  • 2 remained in progress; and
  • 8 were waived.


Infringement amounts vary depending on the nature and severity of the offence and may be either $210 or $1,000. 


The total value paid or payable from these infringement notices was reported as $20,890. 


While infringement notices form an important component of Council's compliance response, enforcement outcomes remain dependent on the availability of evidence sufficient to identify a responsible person and support formal action.

 

  1. Volume and Direct Cost to Council

 

  1. What total tonnage/volume of illegally dumped waste was collected and disposed of by Council staff or contractors over the last financial year?

 

Council records illegal dumping incidents and associated clean-up activities; however, tonnage and volume data is not consistently captured across all collection activities. This is because there is no efficient or reliable way to measure the weight or volume of waste from each individual collection. Illegal dumping collections vary significantly, from small items through to larger loads, so measuring each collection would not be practical within current operational arrangements.  

 

For the purpose of providing an indicative volume estimate, if the 4,719 illegal dumping related collections previously reviewed were assumed to average approximately 20 kilograms per collection, this would equate to approximately 95 tonnes of illegally dumped waste. This figure is an estimate only and should not be read as a measured tonnage.

 

  1. What was the total financial cost incurred by Council (including staff labor, tipping/waste transfer fees, equipment, and contractor costs) to collect and process this dumped waste?

 

Illegal dumping imposes a direct financial burden on Council through investigation, collection, disposal and operational response activities. A precise annual cost is not currently available, as costs are not separately captured for every incident and can vary depending on the size, location and type of material collected.

 

Based on the indicative tonnage estimate outlined in 3a, and applying an estimated disposal and transport cost of approximately $300 per tonne, the direct disposal-related cost would be in the order of $28,500. When this is considered together with labour associated with approximately one full-time equivalent resource, equipment, collection activity and related operational costs, the total annual cost to Council is broadly estimated to be in the order of $125,000 to $150,000. 

 

This estimate should be treated as a broad indication only rather than a fully verified annual expenditure figure. Actual costs will vary depending on the nature, size and location of each incident, the volume and type of material collected, disposal pathway, labour and equipment requirements, and whether investigation or enforcement activity is required. 

 

It is also important to note that these figures are indicative and should not be taken to mean that all illegally dumped material is sent to landfill. The majority of this material is directed through Council’s Recycling and Waste Centre, where recyclable items are separated and recycled where possible. Items that are suitable for reuse may also be rehomed through charity or other reuse pathways. Council makes every reasonable effort to recover, recycle or reuse material before disposal, which helps reduce the amount ultimately sent to landfill.

  1. What is the average timeframe from when an illegal dumping report is logged (e.g., via the Customer Portal, My Local Services app, or Snap Send Solve) to the completion of the investigation?

Investigations may include site inspections, collection of evidence, witness statements, examination of dumped materials and engagement with alleged offenders. Community Safety Officers are committed to undertaking investigations in a timely manner and aim to have most substantive investigations without significant complexities are completed within 14 days.

For example, if a responsible person has been identified and the rubbish does not pose a public safety risk, the responsible person will be provided the opportunity to reclaim the rubbish which means it will remain on public land while that pursued.

Carried Unanimously

The Strategic and Engagement Committee was held on Monday, 17 August 2026.


Moved: Councillor Nicole MazeikaSeconded: Councillor Peter Ppiros

That having considered the recommendations of the Committee which has read and considered the reports in the agenda related to all items, with the exception of Item 4.1:


4.2. - PRESENTATION - ROAD SAFETY AND TRAFFIC MANAGEMENT PROGRAM - 2026 UPDATE
  
 Motion 
  
 That the Committee recommends that:
 
  1. The report be received and noted.
 
  1. Staff be thanked for their presentation and a copy of the presentation be included in the Minutes.
 
 4.3. - RESPONSE TO PETITION - INSTALLATION OF SPEED REDUCTION MEASURES ALONG HERO WAY, WEST LAKES
 
Motion 
  
 That the Committee recommends to the Council:
 
  1. That permanent traffic calming devices are not warranted at this time, and a temporary Variable Messaging Sign (VMS) be installed as a speed calming measure. 
 
  1. That staff advise the South Australian Police of the reported anti-social driving behaviour.
 
  1. That Council notify the head petitioner of Council's decision, and seek feedback on specific issues to assist council in reporting back to SAPOL.
 
 4.4. - CONSIDERATION OF CONSULTATION OUTCOMES - ROAD CLOSURE AND SALE - PORTION OF ROAD ADJACENT 41-45 BEAUFORT STREET, WOODVILLE PARK 
 
Motion
   
 That the Committee recommends that:
 
  1. The Council notes the statutory consultation undertaken in accordance with Part 3 of the Roads (Opening and Closing) Act 1991 for the proposed closure of a portion of road adjacent 41-45 Beaufort Street, Woodville Park.
 
  1. The Council notes no submissions or objections were received during the consultation period.
 
  1. The Council resolves to make a Road Process Order under Part 3 of the Roads (Opening and Closing) Act 1991 to close the portion of road identified in Appendix 2.
 
  1. The Council authorises the Chief Executive Officer to submit the Road Process Order and all required documentation to the Surveyor-General for consideration by the Minister as shown in Appendix 2.
 
  1. Subject to Ministerial approval and gazettal of the road closure, Council proceeds with the transfer of the closed road to the Registered Proprietor of 41–45 Beaufort Street, Woodville Park in accordance with the Preliminary Agreement previously entered into.
 
  1. The Mayor and Chief Executive Officer be authorised to sign and affix the Common Seal to all documents necessary to give effect to this resolution.
 
 4.5. - ROAD CLOSURE - PORTION OF ROAD ADJACENT 5 GETHING CRESCENT, BOWDEN
  
 Motion
   
 That the Committee recommends that:
 
  1. The Council commence the process in Part 3 of the Roads (Opening and Closing) Act 1991 to consider the potential closure of the portion of land identified as area X and area Y in Appendix 1, including undertaking statutory consultation.
 
  1. The Council enter into a Preliminary Agreement as allowed in Part 3, clause 12 of the Roads (Opening and Closing) Act 1991 to facilitate a potential closure and sale of the road to the Registered Proprietors of 5 Gething Crescent, Bowden for the land value (as determined by independent valuation) plus road closing and land transfer costs, all being subject to the outcome of statutory consultation and if so resolved by Council at a future meeting.
 
  1. Should the road closure proceed, Council resolve - pursuant to section 193 (4a) of the Local Government Act 1999 - to exclude the closed road from Community Land classification, to enable any future transfer to the Purchaser and amalgamation with the adjoining allotments.
 
  1. The Mayor and Chief Executive Officer be authorised to sign and seal all documents necessary to facilitate these actions.
  

Council adopts the recommendations of the Committee as printed in the Minutes of this Committee.

Carried Unanimously

Leave of the meeting was sought to bring forward deputation Item 4.1. Leave was granted.

The Operations Committee was held on Monday, 17 August 2026.

Councillor - Rachele Tullio left the meeting at 7:30 PM.

Moved: Councillor Senthil Chidambaranathan
Seconded: Councillor Edgar Agius

That having considered the recommendations of the Committee which has read and considered the reports in the agenda related to items:

 

4.1. - PRESENTATION - TREE CANOPY IMPROVEMENT STRATEGY - 6 MONTHLY UPDATE
 
Motion 
 
 That the Committee recommends to the Council:
 
  1. That the progress of the implementation of actions contained within the Tree Canopy Improvement Strategy, and the implementation of on-ground tree planting works be noted.
 
  1. That further update reports be presented to the Operations Committee at 6 monthly intervals.
 
  1. That staff be thanked for the presentation and the presentation be included in the minutes.
 
4.2. - STREETSCAPE UPGRADE PROJECTS - QUARTERLY UPDATE REPORT
 
Motion 
 
 That the Committee recommends to the Council:
 
  1. That the report be received and noted. 
 
  1. That Council notes that grant applications have been submitted to the Safer Local Roads and Infrastructure Program ($3 million) and the State Bicycle Fund ($200,000) to support the delivery outcomes of the Chief Street Project.
 
4.3. - ST CLAIR RECREATION CENTRE QUARTERLY REPORT - APRIL, MAY AND JUNE 2026
 
Motion 
 
 That the Committee recommends to the Council:
 
  1. That Council notes the YMCA (SA)'s Performance Report for the April to June 2026 quarter. 
 
  1. That further quarterly reports be presented to the Operations Committee.

 

Council adopts the recommendations of the Committee as printed in the Minutes of this Committee.

Carried Unanimously

Councillor - Rachele Tullio entered the meeting at 7:32 PM.

Following Council's recent endorsement of the Statement of Commitment to Closing the Gap in Western Adelaide (CL 27/01/26, Item 6.5) this report seeks Council endorsement for the City of Charles Sturt to formally participate in the Place-Based Partnership Agreement for Western Suburbs of Adelaide under the National Agreement on Closing the Gap 2020.  It requests authorisation for the Mayor to sign the Agreement and outlines Council’s role in a collaborative, multi-government and Aboriginal-led partnership.



Moved: Councillor Nicole Mazeika
Seconded: Councillor Michael McEwen

Motion

That Council:

  1. Acknowledges the importance of the Place‑Based Partnership Agreement for the Western Suburbs of Adelaide in progressing Closing the Gap outcomes locally, and its alignment with the City of Charles Sturt’s endorsed Statement of Commitment to Closing the Gap in Western Adelaide. 

  2. Authorises the Mayor to sign the Place-Based Partnership Agreement for Western Suburbs of Adelaide on behalf of the City of Charles Sturt, noting that participation is subject to the City of Charles Sturt's legislative obligations and internal governance requirements and does not fetter Council's statutory powers or discretion. 

  3. Notes that any future funding, additional resourcing, data-sharing or other binding commitments arising from the agreement will be subject to separate consideration and approval through the appropriate Council or Executive processes, with operational implementation undertaken by authorised officers following Council endorsement. 

Carried Unanimously

This report seeks to finalise the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Performance Review for 2025/2026. Allison Ashby of Ashby Magro (AM) Consulting has provided a report based on feedback from the Council CEO Review Panel and the survey results collated from the Elected Members, a number of Council Officers and relevant external stakeholders against the agreed criteria and performance plan for 2025/2026 together with the Remuneration Tribunal Determination.

 

In accordance with the Local Government Act 1999 the CEO is recommending that this report be heard in confidence under Section 90(3)(a) as the information the disclosure of which would involve the unreasonable disclosure of information concerning the personal affairs of a person or persons (living or dead).


Moved: Councillor Alice Campbell
Seconded: Councillor Peter Ppiros

Recommendation - Exclusion of the Public (from 8:04 PM)

That:

  1. Pursuant to Section 90(2) of the Local Government Act 1999, Council hereby orders that the public be excluded from attendance at this meeting, with the exception of the General Manager Corporate Services, General Manager City Operations, General Manager City Futures, General Manager Engaged Community, Manager People and Culture, Acting Manager Governance and Risk, Governance Officer, and Allison Ashby (Ashby Magro Consulting) currently in attendance at the meeting, in order to consider ITEM 11.1 - CHIEF EXECUTIVE OFFICER PERFORMANCE REVIEW 2025-2026 in confidence.

  2. In accordance with Section 90(3) of the Local Government Act 1999, Council is satisfied that it is necessary that the public be excluded to consider the information contained in the report ITEM 11.1 - CHIEF EXECUTIVE OFFICER PERFORMANCE REVIEW 2025-2026 on the following grounds:
a.
information the disclosure of which would involve the unreasonable disclosure of information concerning the personal affairs of a person or persons (living or dead).

Recommended Action
  1. Accordingly, on this basis, the principle that meetings of the Council should be conducted in a place open to the public has been outweighed by the need to keep the information or discussion confidential.
Carried Unanimously


Moved: Councillor Alice Campbell
Seconded: Councillor Senthil Chidambaranathan

Motion

  1. That Council endorses the CEO Performance Review Report 2025/2026 from Ashby Magro (AM) Consulting as outlined in Appendix 1 to this report.

  2. That Council acknowledges the CEO has performed his role and duties to the satisfaction of Council measured against the nominated key responsibilities, organisational values, strategic performance objectives and the range of identified professional leadership behaviours.

  3. That the Council endorses the CEO's total remuneration package of $431,303 which falls within the Remuneration Tribunals Determination of the minimum and maximum amounts for the City of Charles Sturt.

  4. That the Council authorise the Mayor to offer the CEO a new employment contract on behalf of Council for a period of five (5) years.

  5. That ITEM 11.1 - CHIEF EXECUTIVE OFFICER PERFORMANCE REVIEW 2025-2026 having been considered in confidence pursuant to section 90(3)(a) of the Local Government Act 1999, the Council hereby orders, in accordance with section 91(7) of the Local Government Act 1999 that the report, appendices and the minutes of this item be kept confidential until the contract of employment documents has been updated and signed by the Mayor and CEO.

Carried

Division called by Councillor Kelly Thomas

Voters
For:Councillor - Edgar Agius, Councillor - Alice Campbell, Councillor - Senthil Chidambaranathan, Councillor - Merlindie Fardone, Councillor - Stuart Ghent, Councillor - Nicholas Le Lacheur, Councillor - Nicole Mazeika, Councillor - Michael McEwen, Councillor - Peter Ppiros, Councillor - Quin Tran, Councillor - Rachele Tullio, Councillor - Kenzie van den Nieuwelaar (12)
Against:Councillor - Kelly Thomas (1)
Not Vote:Mayor Angela Evans (1)
The Motion to Item 11.1. was Carried
